doc.title: Jay Leonhart interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Influences: Ray Brown, Blanton, Pettiford and Mulligan
summary: He explains how Ray Brown's sound shaped his own, mentions Blanton and Oscar Pettiford's melodic lines, and praises Gerry Mulligan's melodiousness.

blocks.x: Well it sure showed me what that bass instrument could be about. The sound, the drive, the beauty, it just overwhelmed me. And so I listened and listened. And to this day the way — the sound that Ray Brown got on that record, is to me the way I want the bass to sound. And sometimes I accuse myself, well why don’t you become an original — why don’t you do — and in many ways I’m very original. I write my own songs, I do a lot of things, I don’t play the same notes that Ray plays, but boy I’m telling you, the spirit of his playing very much permeates my own, and he knows it. He and I have become very good friends, I went up to study with him, and I’ll tell him blankly, I can’t help it if you just played that well, anymore than he can help if Blanton played that well, and he copied Blanton and he admits — he heard Blanton and he said I’ve got to do that. But then Ray started swinging it more. Well I heard Ray and I said oh, that’s how the bass has got to sound. And I naturally fell into my own way of playing and I find I’m really influenced by Oscar Pettiford, the melodicness — the melodicness — what’s the word I’m looking for? Melodious?
Melodiousness. That’s worse. We know what you mean.

But his melodic thinking. And he had a different approach than Ray did of course. But I liked lines that really tied together, that really expressed an idea, that didn’t have to stop halfway through because technically you couldn’t find the next note you were trying to say. Even if it’s simple, just real notes. I mean like Gerry Mulligan, listen to Gerry Mulligan. What makes him outstanding is he learned to use the lower register. And he understood the sonic thing on the baritone, and so he played melodies on the baritone that © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -5-

nobody else quite played. He had a melodiousness to his playing that it just comes through every time you hear — you hear two seconds you know it’s Gerry Mulligan on the baritone, because there’s a sonar — I don’t know any words. Buy a dictionary and learn words like sonorous, melodicness, melodiciticity, melodocity — and use them. So some day, when you do an interview you —
They’ll just come right out. It was very sonorous.
I wasn’t prepared for this. And I’m a writer.
